title: Windsor
sub: Castle, the Long Walk and Eton
train: Waterloo to Windsor & Eton Riverside, direct, about 55 minutes. Or Paddington, change at Slough, to Windsor & Eton Central, about 35 minutes.
cab: About an hour by black cab, door to door. Great for a family or a group.
intro: The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world, a royal town to wander, and Eton just over the river. An easy half day from London.
tips: The castle can close at short notice for royal events, so check before you go.
Changing the Guard happens on set days only, usually late morning. Check the times on the castle website.
Book castle tickets online to skip the queue.

pubs.name: The Two Brewers
pubs.where: 34 Park Street, by the Long Walk
pubs.note: One of the smallest pubs in the country, in a building from 1709. Only nine tables, so book ahead.

pubs.name: The Carpenters Arms
pubs.note: A 16th-century pub on a cobbled lane opposite the castle. Sit outside and look up at the walls.

pubs.name: The Horse & Groom
pubs.note: An early-1700s pub right on the castle's doorstep.

pubs.name: The Duchess of Cambridge
pubs.where: Town centre, a short walk from the castle
pubs.note: Traditional British ales and a beer garden.

pubs.name: The George Inn
pubs.note: Eton's most characterful inn, by the bridge, run by the Windsor & Eton Brewery.

pubs.name: The Waterman's Arms
pubs.note: A 17th-century, dog-friendly pub just over the footbridge.

pubs.name: Windsor & Eton Brewery taproom
pubs.note: Have a pint where it's brewed.

eat.name: The Boatman
eat.note: A historic pub with a terrace right on the Thames. The best spot for eating by the river.

eat.name: Bel & the Dragon
eat.note: Food all day by the Eton bridge, with an all-weather conservatory for the river views in winter.

eat.name: Côte
eat.note: A relaxed French lunch after the castle, and a good excuse to cross the bridge.

eat.name: The Fat Duck, The Waterside Inn and The Hind's Head
eat.note: Two three-Michelin-star restaurants in one small village. Book well ahead.

river.name: John Logie Motorboats
river.note: Hire your own rowing boat or motorboat for an hour.

river.name: French Brothers
river.note: Boat trips on the Thames, from a short return trip to a full-day cruise.

river.name: Windsor Duck Tours
river.note: A trip by road and river in one go. A big hit with kids.

more.name: Legoland Windsor
more.note: The big one for families. It's seasonal, so check the dates.

more.name: Windsor Great Park
more.note: Thousands of acres, with Virginia Water lake and the Savill Garden.

more.name: Windsor Carriages
more.note: See the Great Park by horse-drawn carriage.

more.name: Royal Windsor Racecourse
more.note: Famous for its summer evening race nights.

more.name: Theatre Royal Windsor
more.note: A traditional theatre a few minutes from the castle. Panto season is a big one.

stops.name: Windsor & Eton Central station
stops.note: Start here if you came via Slough. The old Victorian station is now a shopping arcade.

stops.name: Windsor Castle
stops.note: The State Apartments, Queen Mary's Dolls' House and St George's Chapel, where Queen Elizabeth II is buried. Allow two to three hours.

stops.name: The Guildhall and the Crooked House
stops.note: Look for the leaning little tea shop next to the Guildhall, one of the most photographed buildings in town.

stops.name: The Long Walk
stops.note: The famous tree-lined avenue, nearly three miles long, with the castle behind you. Walk as far as you like.

stops.name: Alexandra Gardens and the river
stops.note: Riverside gardens and the boat trips along the Thames, with swans everywhere.

stops.name: Windsor Bridge
stops.note: The pedestrian bridge from Windsor to Eton, with a lovely view back to the castle.

stops.name: Eton High Street and Eton College
stops.note: A pretty high street of old shops and pubs leading to the famous school, where 20 Prime Ministers were educated.

title: Bath
sub: Roman Baths, Georgian crescents, hot springs
train: Paddington to Bath Spa, direct, about 1 hour 20 minutes.
cab: About 2½ hours by black cab. Worth it for a group with luggage or a tour combined with Stonehenge.
intro: A whole city of honey-coloured Georgian stone, built around the hot springs the Romans bathed in. Everything is walkable from the station.
tips: Go to the Thermae rooftop pool at dusk for the best view.
The Roman Baths get busy at midday; go early or late.
Try a Sally Lunn's bun, a Bath speciality since the 1600s.

pubs.name: The Star Inn
pubs.note: One of Bath's most historic pubs, with its old wooden benches and panelled rooms still in place.

pubs.name: The Old Green Tree
pubs.note: A tiny, wood-panelled pub in the centre. Snug, old-fashioned and full of character.

pubs.name: The Coeur de Lion
pubs.note: Said to be Bath's smallest pub, down a little lane near the Guildhall Market. Look for the stained-glass window.

pubs.name: The Saracen's Head
pubs.note: One of the oldest pubs in the city. Charles Dickens is said to have stayed here.

pubs.name: The Raven
pubs.note: A proper real-ale pub, famous for its pies.

pubs.name: The Boater
pubs.note: A riverside beer garden with a view of the bridge and the weir.

pubs.name: The Bell Inn
pubs.note: Owned by its regulars, with live music most nights.

eat.name: The Pump Room
eat.where: Abbey Church Yard, next to the Roman Baths
eat.note: Afternoon tea in the elegant Georgian hall Jane Austen wrote about, with live music most days. You can taste the spa water too.

eat.name: The Scallop Shell
eat.note: Some of the best fish and chips in the West Country.

eat.name: Sotto Sotto
eat.note: Italian food in candlelit, stone-vaulted cellars a few minutes from the Abbey.

eat.name: The Olive Tree
eat.note: Bath's Michelin-starred restaurant, in a townhouse near the Circus. Book well ahead.

river.name: Pulteney Cruisers
river.note: An hour on the Avon from the weir out to Bathampton and back, with commentary. Trips stop when the river is high.

river.name: Bath Boating Station
river.note: A Victorian boathouse where you can hire punts, rowing boats and canoes. Open spring to autumn.

river.name: Kennet & Avon Canal towpath
river.note: A flat, peaceful walk along the canal to Bathampton, with narrowboats all the way and The George pub at the end.

more.name: The Holburne Museum
more.note: An art museum in a grand Georgian building, with a café looking onto Sydney Gardens.

more.name: Free walking tours
more.where: Outside the Pump Room, Abbey Church Yard
more.note: The Mayor of Bath's guides run free two-hour walks every day. Just turn up, as there's no booking and they don't take tips.

more.name: Prior Park Landscape Garden
more.where: About 1 mile south of the centre
more.note: A National Trust garden with a Palladian bridge and views over the city. Best by cab, as it's a steep walk.

more.name: Theatre Royal Bath
more.note: One of the oldest working theatres in the country, with touring shows and a big panto.

more.name: Bath Christmas Market
more.note: Wooden chalets through the old streets from late November to December. Check the dates, as it gets very busy at weekends.

stops.name: Bath Spa station
stops.note: Brunel's station. The centre is a five-minute walk.

stops.name: The Roman Baths
stops.note: Some of the best-preserved Roman remains in the world, still fed by the hot spring. Allow 1½ hours.

stops.name: Bath Abbey
stops.note: Next door to the Baths. Look for the stone angels climbing ladders on the front.

stops.name: Sally Lunn's
stops.note: One of Bath's oldest houses, famous for its big, light buns.

stops.name: Pulteney Bridge
stops.note: One of only a handful of bridges in the world lined with shops on both sides, over a weir.

stops.name: Jane Austen Centre
stops.note: Austen lived in Bath and set two novels here. Costumed guides and a tea room.

stops.name: The Circus
stops.note: A perfect circle of Georgian townhouses, designed by John Wood the Elder.

stops.name: The Royal Crescent
stops.note: The sweeping curve of 30 houses that sums up Georgian Bath. No. 1 is a museum.

stops.name: Thermae Bath Spa
stops.note: Bathe in the natural hot spring water, with a rooftop pool looking over the city.

title: Oxford
sub: Colleges, Harry Potter and old pubs
train: Paddington to Oxford, about 1 hour. Or Marylebone to Oxford Parkway or Oxford, about 1 hour.
intro: The city of dreaming spires: medieval colleges, the famous libraries, film locations and some of England's oldest pubs, all close together.
tips: Colleges have their own opening times and some charge; check before you go.
Christ Church's Great Hall inspired Hogwarts' dining hall, so book ahead.
The Turf Tavern is hidden down a tiny alley; follow the signs from Holywell Street.
Try punting on the river. The Cherwell Boathouse hires out traditional punts, and it's one of the classic Oxford experiences.

stops.name: Oxford station
stops.note: About 15 minutes' walk to the centre.

stops.name: Oxford Castle
stops.note: A Norman castle and former prison. Climb the Saxon tower for views.

stops.name: Carfax Tower
stops.note: The tower at the old crossroads in the centre. Climb 99 steps for a view of the spires.

stops.name: Covered Market
stops.note: A Georgian market hall of butchers, bakers, cafés and cake shops.

stops.name: Christ Church
stops.note: Oxford's grandest college, with a cathedral and the Great Hall that inspired Hogwarts.

stops.name: Radcliffe Camera
stops.note: The round domed library that is Oxford's most famous sight, next to the Bodleian Library.

stops.name: Bridge of Sighs
stops.note: Hertford College's covered bridge over New College Lane.

stops.name: Turf Tavern
stops.note: A tiny old pub hidden down an alley, with beer gardens under the old city wall.

stops.name: Ashmolean Museum
stops.note: Britain's oldest public museum, free to enter, with treasures from all over the world.

title: Cambridge
sub: Punting, King's College and the DNA pub
train: King's Cross to Cambridge, fast trains about 50 minutes. Or Liverpool Street, about 1 hour 15 minutes.
intro: Punts gliding past the college lawns, King's College Chapel and the pub where the secret of life was announced. Compact and easy to walk.
tips: Take a punt along the Backs: hire one or go with a guide who tells the stories.
King's College Chapel's choir sings evensong most days in term time, and it's free.
The station is a 25-minute walk from the centre; buses run often.

stops.name: Cambridge station
stops.note: A bus or a 25-minute walk into town.

stops.name: Parker's Piece
stops.note: The open green where some of the first rules of football were written and played, in 1848.

stops.name: Fitzwilliam Museum
stops.note: A grand, free museum of art and antiquities.

stops.name: The Eagle
stops.note: Where Crick and Watson announced in 1953 they had found the secret of life, DNA. Look up at the wartime airmen's graffiti on the ceiling of the RAF bar.

stops.name: Market Square
stops.note: The daily market in the middle of town, good for lunch.

stops.name: King's College Chapel
stops.note: The breathtaking fan-vaulted chapel, home of the famous Christmas Eve carol service.

stops.name: Trinity College
stops.note: Newton's college. The apple tree by the gate is said to be descended from his famous tree.

stops.name: Mathematical Bridge and the punts
stops.note: Queens' College's wooden bridge over the Cam, and the punting stations nearby.

title: Edinburgh
sub: The castle, the Royal Mile and Arthur's Seat
train: King's Cross to Edinburgh Waverley, direct, about 4 hours 20 minutes. Best as an overnight trip.
cab: Too far for a day by road, but we'll take you to King's Cross, Heathrow or the sleeper train at Euston.
intro: Scotland's capital, with a castle on a volcanic rock, the medieval Old Town and Georgian New Town, and an extinct volcano to climb.
tips: In August the Festival and Fringe are on: book well ahead, or avoid if you want it quiet.
Wear good shoes: the Old Town is all hills and cobbles.
The overnight Caledonian Sleeper from Euston gives you a full day.

stops.name: Edinburgh Waverley station
stops.note: Right in the middle of the city, between the Old Town and the New Town.

stops.name: Calton Hill
stops.note: A short climb for one of the best views of the city and its monuments.

stops.name: The Real Mary King's Close
stops.note: Guided tours of the hidden 17th-century streets buried under the Royal Mile.

stops.name: St Giles' Cathedral and the Royal Mile
stops.note: The historic street running from the castle down to the palace, with the cathedral halfway.

stops.name: Victoria Street
stops.note: The curved, colourful street of little shops often linked to Diagon Alley.

stops.name: Edinburgh Castle
stops.note: The castle on the rock, with the Scottish Crown Jewels and the one o'clock gun.

stops.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
stops.note: The King's official residence in Scotland, at the bottom of the Royal Mile.

stops.name: Arthur's Seat
stops.note: An extinct volcano in the middle of the city. About an hour up and down, with amazing views.

title: York
sub: The Minster, the Shambles and the walls
train: King's Cross to York, direct, about 2 hours.
cab: Too far for a day by road, but we'll get you to King's Cross in good time.
intro: A walled medieval city with one of Europe's greatest cathedrals, crooked streets and Viking history, all within a short walk of the station.
tips: Expect a queue at Bettys for afternoon tea; go early or try the smaller branch on Stonegate.
Walk a stretch of the city walls: free, and the best way to see York.
The National Railway Museum, next to the station, is free.

stops.name: York station
stops.note: A grand Victorian station just outside the city walls.

stops.name: National Railway Museum
stops.note: Free, and full of famous locomotives, including royal carriages and a bullet train.

stops.name: City walls at Bootham Bar
stops.note: Climb on to the medieval walls here and walk towards the Minster.

stops.name: York Minster
stops.note: One of the largest Gothic cathedrals in Northern Europe, with huge medieval stained glass.

stops.name: The Shambles
stops.note: A narrow medieval street of overhanging timber buildings, once full of butchers.

stops.name: Jorvik Viking Centre
stops.note: A ride through Viking York, built on the site where it was dug up.

stops.name: Clifford's Tower
stops.note: What's left of York Castle, on its mound, with views from the top.

stops.name: Bettys
stops.note: The famous tea room, with cakes and afternoon tea in an Art Deco room.

title: Stonehenge & Salisbury
sub: The stones, the cathedral and Magna Carta
train: Waterloo to Salisbury, direct, about 1 hour 30 minutes. Then the Stonehenge tour bus from outside Salisbury station.
cab: About 2 hours by black cab to the stones. A cab lets you do Stonehenge and Salisbury, or Stonehenge and Bath, in one day without tour buses.
intro: The world's most famous stone circle, and a cathedral city with Britain's tallest spire and one of the four surviving original Magna Cartas.
tips: Book a timed Stonehenge ticket in advance.
At the summer solstice, sunrise at the stones is a famous, free event.
It's windy and open at the stones; bring a coat even in summer.

stops.name: Salisbury station
stops.note: Buses to Stonehenge leave from outside the station.

stops.name: Market Place
stops.note: Salisbury's market square, with markets on Tuesdays and Saturdays.

stops.name: Salisbury Cathedral
stops.note: Britain's tallest spire, what is said to be the world's oldest working clock, and an original Magna Carta of 1215.

stops.name: Old Sarum
stops.note: The hilltop where Salisbury began: Iron Age earthworks and the ruins of a castle and the first cathedral.

stops.name: Stonehenge visitor centre
stops.note: The exhibition and the reconstructed Neolithic houses. A shuttle takes you to the stones.

stops.name: Stonehenge
stops.note: The great stone circle, built in stages about 5,000 to 4,000 years ago.

title: Brighton
sub: The pier, the Pavilion and the Lanes
train: Victoria or London Bridge to Brighton, direct, about 1 hour.
intro: London's favourite seaside escape: a pebble beach, the pier, an extraordinary royal palace and lanes full of independent shops.
tips: Fish and chips on the beach is a must; watch out for the seagulls.
The Lanes and North Laine are best for shopping; North Laine is quirkier.
Trains back to London run late, so make an evening of it.

stops.name: Brighton station
stops.note: Walk downhill to the sea: about 15 minutes.

stops.name: North Laine
stops.note: Colourful streets of independent shops, vintage clothes and cafés.

stops.name: Royal Pavilion
stops.note: George IV's seaside palace, with Indian domes outside and Chinese-style rooms inside.

stops.name: The Lanes
stops.note: Narrow old alleys full of jewellers, antiques and little restaurants.

stops.name: Brighton Palace Pier
stops.note: The classic pier, with rides, arcades and doughnuts.

stops.name: West Pier ruins
stops.note: The haunting iron skeleton of the old pier, standing in the sea.

stops.name: Brighton i360
stops.note: A glass pod that rises up a tall tower for views along the coast.

title: Canterbury
sub: The cathedral, the river and the old city
train: St Pancras to Canterbury West on the high-speed train, about 55 minutes.
intro: A medieval walled city around England's mother cathedral, where Thomas Becket was murdered in 1170 and pilgrims have come ever since.
tips: The cathedral charges for entry; it's worth it, and services are free to attend.
A punt or rowing trip along the Stour is a lovely way to see the old city.
The Goods Shed by Canterbury West is a great farmers' market and restaurant.

stops.name: Canterbury West station
stops.note: The high-speed trains from St Pancras arrive here.

stops.name: The Goods Shed
stops.note: A farmers' market and restaurant in an old railway goods shed.

stops.name: Westgate Towers
stops.note: England's largest surviving medieval city gate, with gardens beside the river.

stops.name: River Stour boat trips
stops.note: Punts and rowing boats leave from near the old Weavers' houses.

stops.name: Canterbury Cathedral
stops.note: Founded in 597, the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury, and where Becket was murdered.

stops.name: St Augustine's Abbey
stops.note: The ruins of the abbey founded by St Augustine, part of a World Heritage Site with the cathedral.
